clue.text: Transferred back as unwanted

indicators.note: back tells us to read the synonym for transferred from right to left

parts.note: transferred, as data or software moved to another system, is ported

explanation.surface: Someone moved to another post is told they were no longer wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns PORTED round. DE TROP is French borrowed into English for someone or something superfluous.
explanation.definitionFit: The borrowed French phrase describes a person who is superfluous or not welcome in company.

clue.text: Cut back on ice, some being cracked

indicators.note: cracked means broken up, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Skaters reduce time on the ice because some of it is cracking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being cracked' rearranges the nine letters of ON ICE SOME. 'on' looks like part of 'Cut back on' but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To economise is to reduce spending, the same as cutting back.

clue.text: Division involving mature chemical substance

indicators.note: involving means enclosing, so one piece is wrapped round the other

parts.note: a rent is a split or tear, a division
to mature is to age

explanation.surface: A university department is working on a mature chemical.
explanation.definitionFit: A reagent is a compound used to cause or detect a chemical reaction.

clue.text: This added by one to letter?

parts.note: a postscript is something added at the end of a letter
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Something tacked on by someone at the end of a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface describes a postscript; 'letter' is the Greek letter the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: Psi is the twenty-third letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Rather restricting the setter? I don't care!

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so one piece is enclosed by the other

parts.note: so what! is a shrugging exclamation of indifference
the setter refers to themself as me, a crossword convention

explanation.surface: A setter shrugs off criticism that they are rather limiting.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adverbs meaning to a moderate degree, as in rather cold or somewhat cold.

clue.text: Comes to a halt, seeing green turf?

indicators.note: to a halt implies draws up, and up in a down clue reads the word upwards

parts.note: comes is draws, as a vehicle draws up or draws near

explanation.surface: A golfer stops on reaching the green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes to a halt' is DRAWS UP; in a down clue UP means DRAWS is written from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: Sward is an expanse of short grass, the same thing as turf on a lawn or green.

clue.text: Produce ring in quarters and celebrate noisily

parts.note: to produce is to make

indicators.note: in places the ring inside the quarters

parts.note: quarters are compass points, here W, E and E
a hoop is a ring

explanation.surface: Someone forges a ring in sections and then celebrates.
explanation.walkthrough: Quarters are compass points; here West, East and East surround the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to celebrate boisterously, though it also has a racier sense.

clue.text: Wife's joint favourite in the dog class?

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for wife; the 's stands for has
the hip is a joint
a favourite is a pet, as teacher's pet

explanation.surface: A wife's favourite cut of meat is entered into a dog show.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the answer as one member of a class of dogs, a racing breed like a small greyhound.
explanation.definitionFit: A whippet is a breed of dog, so it is one belonging to the canine category.

clue.text: Article about woman showing signs of anaemia

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
she refers to a woman

explanation.surface: A news article covers a woman who has anaemia.
explanation.definitionFit: Anaemia makes the face pale, so someone ashen has that deathly pallor.

clue.text: A nation's revolutionary musical work …

indicators.note: revolutionary suggests turning over, so the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

parts.note: the possessive S is kept as a letter of the fodder here

explanation.surface: A country's revolution is commemorated in a piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' shuffles the eight letters of A NATIONS. The ellipsis joins this clue to the next.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonatina is a short or simple sonata, a kind of instrumental composition.

clue.text: … for example, Tippett's piece

definitions.meaning: the composer Michael Tippett was ..., so he is an example of a titled Sir; the 's stands for is
a chess piece shaped like a horse's head

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: the musical work is a composition by Michael Tippett.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis tricks you into reading 'piece' as Tippett's musical piece; it is a chessman. Sir Michael Tippett was an English composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Tippett held a knighthood, and the horse-headed chessman bears the same name.

clue.text: Presage golfer's warning received during broadcast

parts.note: fore is the shout golfers give to warn of an incoming ball

indicators.note: during means within, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: to broadcast seed is to sow it by scattering
received means had, as in had a letter

explanation.surface: A golfer's shouted warning came during a radio programme, as an omen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' looks like radio but is the farming sense of scattering seed by hand.
explanation.definitionFit: To presage something is to give advance warning of it, a synonym of signal beforehand.

clue.text: Time to support publicity on sign inside store

indicators.note: in a down clue, to support means to sit below the other pieces

parts.note: hype is excessive publicity

indicators.note: inside means one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a letter heading
a mark is a sign

explanation.surface: Time is given to advertising a sign in a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue a piece that supports others sits at the bottom of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypermarket is a very large self-service shop, bigger than a supermarket.

clue.text: Long or short underwear

indicators.note: short means cut off before the end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: pants are underwear (in Britain, underpants or knickers)

explanation.surface: A question of whether to choose long johns or briefs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' cuts the last letter from PANTS. 'Long' is the verb: to long or yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: To pant for something is to yearn eagerly for it, an older sense of longing.

clue.text: Duke's handwriting?

definitions.meaning: dukes is slang for ..., as in put up your dukes; the 's stands for is
an informal word for a person's handwriting

explanation.surface: Is this the aristocrat's own penmanship?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duke' is not a nobleman but boxing slang for a hand clenched to punch.
explanation.definitionFit: A clenched hand is called a duke in slang, and one's scrawl is informally one's hand or penmanship.

clue.text: Head playing fiddle runs inside after concert

indicators.note: after means the rest of the pieces follow the concert word

parts.note: a prom is a promenade concert, as at the London Proms
on, as an actor is on stage or a game is on

indicators.note: inside places one piece within the other

parts.note: to fiddle with something is to toy with it
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: The lead violinist plays fiddle, running inside after a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' is a headland, not a leader; a prom is a promenade concert, as at the London Proms.
explanation.definitionFit: A head is a high point of land jutting out into the sea, as in Beachy Head.

clue.text: Jock's expression initially on confronting hobgoblins?

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's exclamation on meeting hobgoblins.
explanation.walkthrough: Jock is a nickname for a Scotsman, and och is a Scottish exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Och is a Scots interjection of surprise or regret, the kind of thing a Scotsman says.

clue.text: Superfluous leftist worker astride horse

indicators.note: astride means straddling, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: a red ant is a kind of ant, and ants are workers; red suggests the political left
a dun is a horse of grey-brown colour

explanation.surface: A left-wing labourer on horseback is no longer needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astride' places RED ANT on either side of DUN; 'leftist worker' reads as a socialist labourer but is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Redundant means no longer needed or more than required, synonyms of excess.

clue.text: Chest prior put out in church office

indicators.note: put out suggests something disturbed or disarranged, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A monastic prior's chest is put outside the church office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out' rearranges the ten letters of CHEST PRIOR.
explanation.definitionFit: The post held by a parish rector is a clerical position in the church.

clue.text: From which spectators watch odd parts of their contest

indicators.note: odd parts are the first, third and fifth letters of their

parts.note: a race is a contest

explanation.surface: Spectators watch portions of their match.
explanation.walkthrough: In British football grounds the terraces are the banks of standing spaces for spectators.
explanation.definitionFit: Football grounds traditionally had stepped banks where the crowd stood to watch.

clue.text: Extra shrewd and shifty

definitions.meaning: in cricket a ... is an extra, a run awarded when the ball is bowled out of the batter's reach
... is British slang for crafty and unscrupulous, as in a ... boy

explanation.surface: Someone is described as exceptionally clever and devious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extra' reads as an intensifier for 'shrewd' but is a cricket noun. A wide boy in Britain is a small-time spiv.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket extra conceded for a bad ball has the same name as a slang word for a sharp operator.

clue.text: Ring producer keeping ring for driver?

indicators.note: keeping means holding within, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: Richard Wagner composed the Ring cycle of operas
O is a ring shape

explanation.surface: A jeweller who makes rings holds onto one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' puts O inside WAGNER. 'Ring producer' suggests a jeweller but means the composer of Der Ring des Nibelungen.
explanation.definitionFit: A wagoner is a person who drives a horse-drawn wagon.

clue.text: For example, Marilyn Monroe's heavenly body

definitions.meaning: Marilyn Monroe is an example of a film celebrity; the 's stands for is
a sun shining in the night sky

explanation.surface: Marilyn Monroe's famous figure is described as divine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heavenly body' looks like a compliment on Monroe's figure; it is a celestial object.
explanation.definitionFit: A screen celebrity and a shining celestial object share one word.

clue.text: Triple crown — one seen in Irish kings' residence

indicators.note: seen in means placed inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: the Hill of Tara was the seat of the high kings of Ireland
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A three-tier crown is displayed at an ancient Irish royal seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' puts I inside TARA. 'Triple crown' is not a sporting feat but the papal crown.
explanation.definitionFit: The papal tiara is a three-tiered crown once worn by popes.

clue.text: Cleansing sailor's flat at last sounds pressing

parts.note: AB is an able seaman, so sailor's gives AB's

indicators.note: at last picks the final letter of flat
sounds signals a word said aloud, giving letters spelt differently

parts.note: pressing means urgent, as in a pressing need

explanation.surface: A sailor's flat finally sounds an urgent call for cleaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounds' gives ERGENT, said like URGENT. AB is the usual abbreviation for an able-bodied seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: An abstergent substance is one that cleans or scours, a rare formal word for detergent.

clue.text: Down-at-heel tramp finally abandons fast

indicators.note: abandons means leaves, so a letter is taken out

parts.note: fast means speedy

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of tramp

explanation.surface: A shabby tramp finally gives up fasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' gives P from tramp; 'abandons' drops it from SPEEDY. 'fast' looks like abstaining from food.
explanation.definitionFit: Seedy means shabby and disreputable, like down-at-heel.

clue.text: Crazy to go back and demand woven fabric

indicators.note: to go back means the word for crazy is read right to left

parts.note: crazy means mad
to demand is to ask for firmly

explanation.surface: Someone foolishly goes back to demand a refund for a woven material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go back' reverses MAD to DAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Damask is a reversible patterned cloth, usually of silk or linen, made on a loom.

clue.text: European sensation after execution is botched

indicators.note: botched means bungled, so the remaining letters are jumbled
execution here is beheading, so the word loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A sensation follows an execution that goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after execution' beheads SENSATION to ENSATION; 'is botched' rearranges those eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonia is a Baltic state, so a native of it is a European.

clue.text: Objection raised regarding subject of Jonson's tale

indicators.note: raised in a down clue means the word is written upward

parts.note: but is an objection, as in no ifs or buts

explanation.surface: An objection is raised about the topic of a Jonson story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns BUT upwards. Ben Jonson wrote the comedy A Tale of a Tub.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Jonson's play A Tale of a Tub takes the vessel as its title subject.

clue.text: Bloke's attempt to secure new place in Northants

parts.note: Dave stands for any ordinary bloke; the 's stands for has
an attempt is a try

explanation.surface: A man tries to buy a new house in a Midlands county town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to secure' puts N inside TRY. Northants is the short form of Northamptonshire, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Daventry is a market town in Northamptonshire in the English Midlands.

clue.text: Extremely bizarre charge for carpet

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes, the first and last letters of bizarre

parts.note: a charge is a rate, the price asked

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the price of a carpet is outrageous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carpet' is the verb: to carpet someone is British slang for reprimanding them, as called onto the boss's carpet.
explanation.definitionFit: To be carpeted is to be scolded by a superior, the same as being told off severely.
